title: Article 3 — Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States

content.overview: Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new States and to alter the areas, boundaries or names of existing States. A Bill for the purpose may be introduced only on the recommendation of the President, and where it affects the area, boundaries or name of a State, the President must refer it to the State Legislature for expressing its views within the period specified (or further allowed).
content.glance: Parliament may form new States / alter area, boundaries or name. Bill only on Presidential recommendation; affected State Legislature must be referred for views (not veto).

sections.heading: Constitutional text (substance)
sections.body:
Parliament may by law form a new State by separation of territory from any State or by uniting two or more States or parts of States or by uniting any territory to a part of any State; increase or diminish the area of any State; alter the boundaries of any State; or alter the name of any State.

Proviso: Bill only on Presidential recommendation; where area/boundaries/name of a State is affected, President shall refer the Bill to that State’s Legislature for expressing its views within the specified (or further allowed) period.

sections.heading: Procedure — recommendation and reference
sections.body:
1. Presidential recommendation is a condition precedent to introduction of the Bill.
2. Reference to the affected State Legislature is mandatory when area, boundaries or name is affected.
3. The State expresses views; it does not have a veto. Parliament may pass the law even if the State disagrees.
4. After the period expires (or views are received), Parliament proceeds under ordinary legislative process.

sections.heading: Exam checkpoints
sections.body:
1. List the five powers (form new State; increase/diminish area; alter boundaries; alter name).
2. Stress: recommendation of President + reference for views (not consent).
3. Cite Article 4: Schedule amendments; not Article 368 amendments.
4. Contrast with classical federal requirement of unit consent for territorial change.

examples.title: Illustration — New State by separation
examples.body: Parliament, on Presidential recommendation and after reference to the affected State Legislature for views, passes a law separating territory from State X to form State Y, amends the First Schedule under Article 4, and provides transitional arrangements. The law is valid under Articles 3 and 4 and is not an Article 368 amendment.

misconceptions.trap: A State can veto its own reorganisation under Article 3.
misconceptions.correction: The State Legislature is only entitled to express its views. Parliament is not bound by those views. There is no State veto.

misconceptions.trap: Article 3 laws are constitutional amendments under Article 368.
misconceptions.correction: Article 4 expressly provides that they are not amendments of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain the power and procedure under Article 3.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new States and to alter the areas, boundaries or names of existing States. A Bill may be introduced only on the recommendation of the President. Where the proposal affects the area, boundaries or name of a State, the President must refer the Bill to that State’s Legislature for expressing its views within the period specified or further allowed. The State’s views are consultative, not binding. Under Article 4, such a law may amend the First and Fourth Schedules and is not an amendment under Article 368.

examTips: Emphasise: Presidential recommendation + reference for views (no veto). Always link Art 4.

Bill only on Presidential recommendation; affected State is referred for views (not veto).
